name: Unfolding a recurrence
quick: Substitute the recurrence repeatedly to expose accumulated contributions.
definition: Each substitution moves to an earlier index and adds a contribution or factor. Stop at a defined initial term and count the substitutions.
confusion: A chain displaying $a_{n-3}$ requires n at least 3; small inputs stop sooner.

name: Conjecture
quick: A proposed claim not yet established by proof.
definition: Patterns in computed terms can suggest a formula. Verify its initial values and update rule before treating it as a theorem.
example: Terms 3,7,15 suggest $2^{n+1}-1$ under the appropriate indexing.
confusion: Agreement on finitely many terms does not prove agreement forever.

name: First-order recurrence
quick: A recurrence reaching back one index.
definition: An explicit first-order rule determines each term from its predecessor and stated data. With a valid initial value and domain, repeated application determines the sequence.
confusion: Order describes the furthest index needed, not the degree of n in a formula.

name: Linear recurrence
quick: Earlier sequence values enter only as first powers with coefficients independent of those values.
definition: In a linear recurrence, earlier sequence values appear only to the first power, multiplied by coefficients independent of those values, and added together; an extra term depending on the index is allowed. Coefficients may in general depend on the index. This lesson uses fixed coefficients. Products or squares of earlier sequence values would be nonlinear.
confusion: “Linear recurrence” does not mean its solution grows linearly in n.

name: Homogeneous recurrence
quick: A linear recurrence with no extra contribution independent of earlier sequence values.
definition: A linear recurrence is homogeneous when its update combines earlier sequence values only. A nonhomogeneous rule adds a contribution independent of those sequence values, such as a fixed constant or a specified function of the index.
example: $a_n=2a_{n-1}$ is homogeneous; adding 3 makes it nonhomogeneous.
confusion: A homogeneous recurrence may have nonzero initial values.

name: Equilibrium of an update
quick: A constant value unchanged by the recurrence.
definition: For $a_n=ra_{n-1}+b$, solve $L=rL+b$. Subtracting L leaves the homogeneous update $a_n-L=r(a_{n-1}-L)$.
example: For $a_n=a_{n-1}/2+2$, L=4 and differences from 4 halve.
confusion: An equilibrium need not equal the sequence’s initial value or attract every sequence.

name: Normalization of a recurrence
quick: Change variables to remove a known factor.
definition: Here normalization divides a_n by a nonzero exponential factor so the new sequence has a simpler update. Restore the original factor after solving.
confusion: Division needs a nonzero factor and the new initial value must be checked.

name: Weighted contribution
quick: An added term multiplied by its subsequent update factors.
definition: In $a_n=ra_{n-1}+f(n)$, the contribution f(j) is multiplied by r at each of the n-j later steps, giving $r^{n-j}f(j)$.
example: At step 3, a contribution from step 1 receives the factor $r^2$.
confusion: The newest contribution has weight 1, not r.

name: Second-order recurrence
quick: A rule reaching back two indices.
definition: The fixed-coefficient homogeneous form is $a_n=pa_{n-1}+qa_{n-2}$ for n at least 2, with specified a0 and a1.
confusion: One initial value usually cannot select a unique solution.

name: Characteristic equation
quick: An algebraic equation for geometric solution bases.
definition: Trying $a_n=r^n$ in a second-order homogeneous rule gives $r^2-pr-q=0$ for nonzero r; zero roots are handled separately. Distinct roots provide geometric solutions whose coefficients fit initial data.
example: For coefficients 5 and -6, $(r-2)(r-3)=0$ gives bases 2 and 3.
confusion: Roots determine candidate shapes; initial values determine their coefficients.

name: Repeated characteristic root
quick: The same root appears twice in the characteristic polynomial.
definition: For a nonzero repeated real root $\rho$, use the candidate $(A+Bn)\rho^n$, where $A,B$ are constants chosen to match the two initial values and $n$ is the nonnegative integer index. Dividing by $\rho^n$ turns the recurrence into constant consecutive differences.
example: For repeated root 2 and initial values 1,6, the result is $(1+2n)2^n$.
confusion: Two constant multiples of the same geometric sequence combine into one and cannot fit arbitrary two-value data.

name: Rho
quick: $\rho$ names the repeated root in this lesson.
definition: The Greek letter rho is a real constant here. It is distinct from the running integer index n and the fitted constants A,B.
confusion: The nonzero assumption is required before dividing by powers of rho.

name: Optimality
section: A recurrence for a recursive construction
quick: No permitted solution improves on the claimed minimum cost.
definition: A construction gives an upper bound on the minimum. A lower bound applying to every legal strategy is also needed to prove optimality.
example: A Hanoi construction uses $2^n-1$ moves; the largest-disk argument proves every solution needs at least that many.
confusion: Solving the cost recurrence for one algorithm does not prove it optimal among all algorithms.

name: Tower of Hanoi
section: A recurrence for a recursive construction
quick: Move ordered disks among three pegs, one exposed disk at a time.
definition: Disks have distinct sizes. Never put a larger disk on a smaller one. Transfer the whole stack to another peg; the minimum satisfies H0=0 and Hn=2H(n-1)+1.
example: Two disks need three moves: small aside, large to target, small onto large.
confusion: A legal strategy’s move count alone supplies only an upper bound.

name: Divide and conquer
quick: Solve smaller subproblems and combine their results.
definition: A cost recurrence counts all child calls plus the work done at the current call. State subproblem sizes and rounding rules.
example: $T(n)=2T(n/2)+n$ models two equal halves plus n units of local work on powers of two.
confusion: Halving alone does not determine cost; the number of children matters.

name: Recursion tree
quick: One node per call, connected to the calls it makes.
definition: Level j counts connections from the original call, whose level is zero. Leaves make no further calls. Sum local work at all nodes, including leaves.
example: For size 8 split in half twice per call, levels have 1,2,4,8 calls.
confusion: Depth counts the longest route, not the total number of calls.

name: Base-2 logarithm
quick: $\log_2 n$ is the exponent producing n as a power of 2.
definition: For n=2^k, the logarithm equals k and counts exact halvings down to 1. Only positive n have real logarithms.
confusion: For non-powers of two, integer step counts require floor or ceiling conventions.

name: Merge sort
quick: Sort smaller halves, then merge their ordered results.
definition: Merging repeatedly takes the smaller next item from two sorted lists to produce one sorted list. A cost model must count actual operations and base work.
confusion: An idealized exact n merge cost need not match every implementation.

name: Recurrence from counting
quick: Count objects by splitting them into disjoint cases described by smaller instances.
definition: Choose cases that cover every object exactly once. Relate each case to objects of a smaller size, then add their counts. Supply the initial counts separately; the same update rule can describe different sequences.
example: For binary strings with no adjacent ones, an ending 0 leaves any valid shorter string. An ending 1 must follow 0, except at length one. Thus $F_n=F_{n-1}+F_{n-2}$ for $n\geq2$, with $F_0=1$ and $F_1=2$.
confusion: The update resembles the Fibonacci rule, but these initial values count a different sequence. Overlapping cases would double-count objects.
